imo-1991-01.title: Compute the ratios, then AM–GM
imo-1991-01.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$ and $p=a+b+c$.

**The ratio $AI/AA'$.** By the angle bisector theorem, $BA'=\dfrac{ac}{b+c}$. In triangle $ABA'$, $BI$ bisects the angle at $B$, so
$$\frac{AI}{IA'}=\frac{AB}{BA'}=\frac{c(b+c)}{ac}=\frac{b+c}{a},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad \frac{AI}{AA'}=\frac{b+c}{a+b+c}.$$
Similarly $\dfrac{BI}{BB'}=\dfrac{c+a}{p}$ and $\dfrac{CI}{CC'}=\dfrac{a+b}{p}$. Put
$$x=\frac{b+c}{p},\quad y=\frac{c+a}{p},\quad z=\frac{a+b}{p},\qquad x+y+z=2.$$
The quantity in the problem is $xyz$.

**Upper bound.** By AM–GM, $xyz\le\left(\dfrac{x+y+z}{3}\right)^3=\dfrac{8}{27}$ (equality for the equilateral triangle).

**Lower bound.** By the triangle inequality $a<b+c$, so $x=\frac{b+c}{p}>\frac12$; likewise $y,z>\frac12$. Write $x=\frac12+u$, $y=\frac12+v$, $z=\frac12+w$ with $u,v,w>0$ and $u+v+w=2-\frac32=\frac12$. Then
$$xyz=\frac18+\frac{u+v+w}{4}+\frac{uv+vw+wu}{2}+uvw>\frac18+\frac18=\frac14 .$$
∎

imo-1991-02.title: Look at the smallest prime not dividing $n$
imo-1991-02.body:
Clearly $a_1=1$ and $a_k=n-1$. Since $n>6$, $\varphi(n)=k\ge 3$ (only $n\le 6$, namely $n=3,4,6$, have $\varphi(n)=2$). The second term $a_2$ is the smallest integer $>1$ coprime to $n$, which is the smallest prime $p$ not dividing $n$. So the common difference is $d=p-1$ and $a_i=1+(i-1)(p-1)$.

**$p=2$.** Then $d=1$: every number $1,2,\dots,n-1$ is coprime to $n$, so $n$ is prime.

**$p=3$.** Then $2\mid n$ and $d=2$: the totatives are exactly the odd numbers $1,3,5,\dots,n-1$. If $n$ had an odd prime factor $q$, then $q<n$ would be an odd number less than $n$ not coprime to $n$ — contradiction. So $n$ is a power of $2$.

**$p\ge5$.** Then $2\mid n$ and $3\mid n$. Since $n-1=a_k=1+(k-1)(p-1)$, we get $(p-1)\mid n-2$. But $n-2\equiv1\pmod 3$, so $3\nmid p-1$; as $p\ne3$ this means $p\equiv2\pmod 3$. Because $k\ge3$, the number $a_3=2p-1$ is a totative, yet $2p-1\equiv 4-1\equiv0\pmod3$ and $3\mid n$ — contradiction.

Hence $n$ is a prime or a power of $2$. ∎

imo-1991-03.title: Extremal set plus eight disjoint coprime quintuples
imo-1991-03.body:
**A set of $216$ elements with no five pairwise coprime numbers.** Let $A$ be the set of numbers in $S$ divisible by at least one of $2,3,5,7$. By inclusion–exclusion,
$$|A|=(140+93+56+40)-(46+28+20+18+13+8)+(9+6+4+2)-1=329-133+21-1=216.$$
Among any five elements of $A$, two are divisible by the same prime from $\{2,3,5,7\}$ (pigeonhole), so they are not coprime. Hence $n\ge217$.

**Every $217$-element subset works.** Let $T$ be the set consisting of $1$ and all primes in $S$; there are $59$ primes up to $280$, so $|T|=60$ and $|S\setminus T|=220$. Any numbers from $T$ are pairwise coprime. Let $X\subseteq S$ with $|X|=217$.
- If $|X\cap T|\ge5$ we are done.
- Otherwise $|X\cap (S\setminus T)|\ge 213$, so at most $7$ elements of $S\setminus T$ are missing from $X$.

Now consider the following eight disjoint sets of composite numbers in $S$; within each set the numbers are pairwise coprime (the prime factors used in each set are all different):
$$\begin{aligned}
&\{2\cdot23,\ 3\cdot19,\ 5\cdot17,\ 7\cdot13,\ 11\cdot11\},&&\{2\cdot29,\ 3\cdot23,\ 5\cdot19,\ 7\cdot17,\ 11\cdot13\},\\
&\{2\cdot31,\ 3\cdot29,\ 5\cdot23,\ 7\cdot19,\ 11\cdot17\},&&\{2\cdot37,\ 3\cdot31,\ 5\cdot29,\ 7\cdot23,\ 11\cdot19\},\\
&\{2\cdot41,\ 3\cdot37,\ 5\cdot31,\ 7\cdot29,\ 11\cdot23\},&&\{2\cdot43,\ 3\cdot41,\ 5\cdot37,\ 7\cdot31,\ 13\cdot13\},\\
&\{2\cdot47,\ 3\cdot43,\ 5\cdot41,\ 7\cdot37,\ 13\cdot17\},&&\{2^2,\ 3^2,\ 5^2,\ 7^2,\ 13\cdot19\}.
\end{aligned}$$
(The largest of these numbers is $7\cdot37=259\le280$.) Since $X$ misses at most $7$ elements of $S\setminus T$, and the eight sets are disjoint, one of them lies entirely in $X$, giving five pairwise coprime numbers.

**Answer: $217$.**

imo-1991-04.title: Label along trails
imo-1991-04.body:
If $k=0$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise pick a vertex $v_0$ with at least one edge and label as follows, using the labels $1,2,3,\dots$ in order.

**Procedure.** Starting at $v_0$, walk along unlabeled edges, giving each edge the next label, until you reach a vertex with no unlabeled edges. Then, if unlabeled edges remain, choose a vertex that is already *touched* (an endpoint of a labeled edge) and has an unlabeled edge, and start a new walk from there, continuing the numbering. Repeat until all edges are labeled.

**Such a restart vertex always exists.** Suppose some edge $xy$ is unlabeled. Take a path $v_0=w_0,w_1,\dots,w_r=x$ (connectivity), followed by the edge $xy$. Let $w_iw_{i+1}$ be the first unlabeled edge on this walk; $w_i$ is $v_0$ or an endpoint of the labeled edge $w_{i-1}w_i$, so it is touched and has an unlabeled edge.

**The gcd condition.** The vertex $v_0$ lies on the edge labeled $1$, so the gcd at $v_0$ is $1$. Let $u\ne v_0$ be a vertex of degree $\ge2$. Every walk starts at a touched vertex, so $u$ becomes touched for the first time by being *entered* along some walk, via an edge with label $i$. At that moment the edge with label $i$ is the only labeled edge at $u$, and $u$ has another (unlabeled) edge, so the walk is not stuck and leaves $u$ along an edge labeled $i+1$. Since $\gcd(i,i+1)=1$, the gcd of all labels at $u$ is $1$.

All $k$ edges receive the labels $1,\dots,k$, and the condition holds at every vertex of degree at least $2$. ∎

imo-1991-05.title: Trigonometric Ceva and Jensen
imo-1991-05.body:
Let
$$\alpha_1=\angle PAB,\ \alpha_2=\angle PAC,\quad \beta_1=\angle PBC,\ \beta_2=\angle PBA,\quad \gamma_1=\angle PCA,\ \gamma_2=\angle PCB .$$
All six are positive and their sum is $\angle A+\angle B+\angle C=180^\circ$.

**Trigonometric Ceva.** The law of sines in triangles $PAB$, $PBC$, $PCA$ gives
$$\frac{PA}{PB}=\frac{\sin\beta_2}{\sin\alpha_1},\qquad\frac{PB}{PC}=\frac{\sin\gamma_2}{\sin\beta_1},\qquad\frac{PC}{PA}=\frac{\sin\alpha_2}{\sin\gamma_1}.$$
Multiplying, $\sin\alpha_1\sin\beta_1\sin\gamma_1=\sin\alpha_2\sin\beta_2\sin\gamma_2$.

**Bound.** Hence, using AM–GM and then the concavity of $\sin$ on $[0,\pi]$ (Jensen),
$$(\sin\alpha_1\sin\beta_1\sin\gamma_1)^2=\prod_{\text{all six}}\sin\theta\le\Big(\frac{\sum\sin\theta}{6}\Big)^6\le\Big(\sin\frac{\sum\theta}{6}\Big)^6=\sin^6 30^\circ=\frac1{64}.$$
So $\sin\alpha_1\sin\beta_1\sin\gamma_1\le\frac18$ and one of the three sines, say $\sin\theta$ with $\theta\in\{\alpha_1,\beta_1,\gamma_1\}$, is $\le\frac12$. Then $\theta\le30^\circ$ or $\theta\ge150^\circ$.

**Excluding $\theta\ge150^\circ$.** Suppose e.g. $\alpha_1\ge150^\circ$. Then $\angle A>\alpha_1\ge150^\circ$, so $\angle B<30^\circ$ and $\beta_1<\angle B<30^\circ$. The cases $\beta_1\ge150^\circ$ (then $\gamma_1<\angle C<30^\circ$) and $\gamma_1\ge150^\circ$ (then $\alpha_1<\angle A<30^\circ$) are the same.

In every case one of $\angle PAB,\angle PBC,\angle PCA$ is at most $30^\circ$. ∎

imo-1991-06.title: Fractional parts of multiples of $\sqrt2$
imo-1991-06.body:
Let $\{t\}=t-\lfloor t\rfloor$ denote the fractional part and define
$$x_i=4\{i\sqrt2\}\qquad(i\ge0).$$
Clearly $0\le x_i<4$, so the sequence is bounded.

**Lemma.** For every integer $k\ge1$ and every integer $m$, $|k\sqrt2-m|>\dfrac{1}{4k}$.

*Proof.* If $|k\sqrt2-m|\ge1$ this is clear. Otherwise $0<k\sqrt2-1<m<k\sqrt2+1$, so $0<k\sqrt2+m<2\sqrt2k+1<4k$. Since $\sqrt2$ is irrational, $2k^2-m^2$ is a nonzero integer, so
$$|k\sqrt2-m|=\frac{|2k^2-m^2|}{k\sqrt2+m}\ge\frac{1}{k\sqrt2+m}>\frac{1}{4k}.\qquad\square$$

**Verification.** Let $i\ne j$, $k=|i-j|\ge1$. Then
$$\{i\sqrt2\}-\{j\sqrt2\}=(i-j)\sqrt2-\big(\lfloor i\sqrt2\rfloor-\lfloor j\sqrt2\rfloor\big)=\pm(k\sqrt2-m)$$
for some integer $m$. By the lemma $|x_i-x_j|=4|k\sqrt2-m|>\dfrac1k$. Therefore
$$|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^a>\frac{1}{k}\cdot k^a=k^{a-1}\ge1,$$
because $a>1$ and $k\ge1$. ∎

*(Remark: the same sequence even works for $a=1$.)*
